title: Smart or Bluetooth speaker: battery, drivers, magnets and amplifier board
summary: A smart or Bluetooth speaker gives you one or more good speaker drivers with neodymium magnets, a small amplifier board, tiny microphones and, in portable models, a lithium battery. Allow about 25 minutes: the case is usually glued and the screws hide under rubber. The main danger is the lithium cell: don't pierce, bend or short it.

steps.text: Unplug it and set the power adapter aside. If the mains lead goes straight into the body (no separate adapter), leave it unplugged for 10 minutes before opening and don't touch the power supply board inside.
steps.warn: Models with a built-in mains supply have a high-voltage capacitor that holds its charge. Leave that board alone unless you have discharged it (see safety_discharge_capacitor).

steps.text: Check the case for swelling: a bulged base, a seam pushed open, a warm case or a sweet chemical smell all mean a swollen lithium cell. Take the speaker outdoors and read safety_swollen_lithium before going on.

Find the screws. They hide under the rubber base (peel it up from one edge), under the fabric grille, beneath stickers and under rubber end caps. Screws may be Phillips, Torx or security types. If you find none, the seam is glued: slide a thin plastic pry tool along it and work round a little at a time.
steps.warn: The battery sits right behind the shell. Keep any blade shallow and never push a knife into the seam: it can slice a battery.

steps.text: Open it slowly and photograph how it lies before you move anything. Flat ribbon cables have a small locking flap: flip it up and slide the cable out. Other connectors unclip.
Disconnect the battery before anything else: pull its plug by the plastic housing, never by the wires. If the leads are soldered, cut them one at a time and tape each end at once.
steps.warn: A short across a lithium pack can heat the wires red and start a fire. Never cut both leads in one go, and never let bare ends touch.

steps.text: Take the battery out. Cylindrical cells slide out of a holder. A flat pouch pack is stuck down: lift one edge with a plastic card, never a metal blade, and don't bend or fold it. If it won't come, leave it in the case and take everything else out. Read the capacity and voltage printed on it and test it as in test_lithium_cell.
steps.warn: A dented or punctured pouch cell can ignite minutes later. Use plastic tools only, and put it on bare ground or in a metal tin away from anything that burns.

steps.text: Free the speaker drivers: undo the 3-4 screws round each frame, or cut through the glue ring, and lift them out. Cut the two wires about 5 cm from the driver, or unplug the small connector. Don't press on the cone. Round or oval cones with no wires are passive radiators: a weighted cone with no magnet.
Leave each magnet fitted. It is glued in a steel cup at the back of the driver, and the driver is far more useful whole. Keep drivers face-down and well apart.
steps.warn: Two bare magnets slam together and pinch hard. Keep them apart with a spacer and away from compasses, cards and anyone with a pacemaker.

steps.text: Lift out the top board: it carries the touch controls, the LED ring or status LEDs and, on smart models, an array of 4-7 tiny microphones. Keep it whole and note which cable goes where. The microphones are very small: don't try to pull them off one by one.

Take out the main board with its power jack: undo its screws and unplug it. It holds the amplifier (a small chip, often with a flat metal pad on the board), the radio, the charging chip and the battery protection. Keep the amplifier section on the board; it is a ready-made small amplifier. If there is a touchscreen, lift it off gently: its ribbon cable tears easily.
Keep the power adapter and its lead. Read the volts and amps off its label: 12-21 V is usual for smart speakers and 5 V for USB models. It is a spare supply for other projects.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Drivers.** Full-range speakers from 2 to 30 W: replace a dead radio speaker, build a small stereo pair, or put one in a box with the amplifier board. Test a driver by touching a 1.5 V cell across its two leads for a moment: the cone should push out or click.
- **Amplifier board.** Bluetooth speaker boards often still work as a powered Bluetooth receiver and amplifier once you give them 5 V or reconnect the battery. Smart (Wi-Fi) speaker boards often won't start without the maker's service, but the amplifier chip may still be usable by a person who can read its data sheet.
- **Battery.** Cylindrical cells (often 18650) can go into packs or lamps (see build_18650_pack and test_lithium_cell). Pouch packs have a protection board attached; keep it with the cell.
- **Magnets.** Neodymium rings or discs behind each driver, useful for small generators, latches and pickup tools. Leave them on the driver unless you need them bare.
- **Microphones.** Many smart speaker microphones are MEMS parts with digital output: they need a microcontroller to read. Keep the board whole.
- **LED ring.** Small RGB LEDs with a driver chip. Use as a status light.
- **Power adapter.** 5 V USB or 12-21 V barrel plug: a handy supply for small projects (see build_usb_charging_station for charging uses).

## Variations

- Smart displays have a touchscreen and a camera module as well. Leave the camera cable alone until you have the case open and the battery out.
- High-end speakers (Sonos, HomePod and similar) have mains supplies inside and several powered drivers.
- Cheap portable speakers often hold only one small driver, a pouch cell and a tiny board; the whole job takes 10 minutes.

## What to leave

- A swollen or punctured battery: see safety_swollen_lithium.
- Any internal mains power supply you haven't discharged.
- The plastic shell and fabric grille.
